title: What a 510 Cartridge Is
summary: 510 is a thread size, not a brand: ten threads of half a millimetre each, the informal standard that lets almost any cartridge screw onto almost any battery. It says nothing about what is inside the cartridge, how well it is built, or how it will perform.
body: The number describes a screw thread and nothing else. Once you know that, most of the confusion around cartridges and batteries goes away.
## Where the name comes from

Ten threads, each 0.5 mm in pitch — 5-10. It began as one manufacturer's connector and became the de facto standard because everyone copied it, which is why a cartridge bought from one company usually fits a battery bought from another.
It is a convention rather than a certified standard. Nobody administers it, nothing is tested against it, and "510 compatible" is a claim about geometry, not about quality.
## What the parts are

| Part | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Cartridge** | Holds the contents, the wick and the heating element. Consumable. |
| **Battery** | Supplies power. Reusable. Often called a pen. |
| **510 connection** | The threaded joint between them. |
| **Mouthpiece** | Usually moulded into the cartridge, sometimes separate. |
## What 510 does not tell you

- **Nothing about the heating element.** Ceramic, quartz and wick-and-coil all come in 510 cartridges and behave differently. See [what a coil does and why material matters](/blog/what-a-coil-does-and-why-material-matters).
- **Nothing about voltage.** A battery set too high for a given cartridge scorches it; too low and it barely warms. Variable-voltage batteries exist for this reason.
- **Nothing about the seals.** Leaking is a build-quality question, and build quality varies enormously between cartridges that thread identically.
- **Nothing about capacity.** 0.5 g, 1 g and 2 g cartridges all use the same thread.
## Fitting one

**Hand tight only.** The commonest hardware failure we hear about is a cartridge cross-threaded or over-tightened until the centre pin is crushed, after which it will not make contact on any battery. Turn until it stops, then stop.
If it will not sit flush, back it out fully and start again rather than forcing it — the thread is soft metal and it strips.
## Disposable versus cartridge

A disposable is the same arrangement with the battery sealed to the cartridge and no thread at all. Which you are holding changes what you can do when something goes wrong. See [disposable or cartridge, what the difference is](/blog/disposable-or-cartridge-what-the-difference-is).

title: Disposable or Cartridge: What the Difference Is
summary: A disposable is one sealed unit — battery, cartridge and contents together, discarded when empty. A cartridge is the consumable half only, screwed onto a battery you keep. The first is simpler; the second is cheaper over time and easier to diagnose when something stops working.
body: Two formats, and most of the practical differences follow from one fact: whether the battery is replaceable.
## Side by side

| Aspect | Disposable | Cartridge plus battery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Battery | Sealed inside, discarded with it | Kept and reused |
| Contents | Fixed at manufacture | You choose each cartridge |
| Cost per unit | Lower up front | Higher up front, lower over time |
| Voltage control | Rarely any | Common on better batteries |
| If it stops working | The whole thing is scrap | Swap parts to find the fault |
| Waste | A lithium cell every time | One cell for many cartridges |
## Rechargeable disposables

A middle category, and the source of most of the confusion. These are sealed like a disposable but carry a USB-C port so the battery can be topped up — because the cell is smaller than the contents it has to heat, and would otherwise die with the device half full.
Charging one is not the same as charging a phone. See [charging a rechargeable device safely](/blog/charging-a-rechargeable-device-safely).
## Diagnosing a fault

This is the real argument for the two-part format. When a cartridge-and-battery setup stops working you can isolate the cause: another cartridge on the same battery, or the same cartridge on another battery, tells you which half failed in thirty seconds.

A sealed disposable gives you no such test. A blinking light is the only information you get, and it means several different things. See [what a blinking light usually means](/blog/what-a-blinking-light-usually-means).
## Which to buy
Buy a **disposable** when you want nothing to think about, or to try something once.

Buy a **cartridge and battery** when you expect to buy more than a few, when you want control over voltage, or when you would rather not throw a lithium cell away every time. Either way, the hardware and the contents are separate questions — the thread standard says nothing about what is in the tank. See [what a 510 cartridge is](/blog/the-510-thread-explained).
## Disposal
Both formats end as electronic waste with a lithium cell in them, which is not household rubbish. See [disposing of hardware and lithium batteries](/blog/disposing-of-hardware-and-lithium-batteries).

title: What a Coil Does, and Why the Material Matters
summary: The heating element turns battery power into heat, and what it is made of decides how evenly that heat arrives. Ceramic elements spread it and run cooler; bare wire on cotton wick heats fast and scorches easily. Most complaints about taste are really complaints about the element.
body: Every cartridge contains a heating element and something to carry liquid to it. Those two parts, not the branding on the box, decide what the device is like to use.
## The three arrangements

| Element | How it behaves |
| --- | --- |
| **Ceramic** | Heat spreads through a porous block. Even, slower to start, tolerant of thicker contents. |
| **Quartz rod with wire** | Heats very fast, cools fast, less even. |
| **Wire coil on cotton wick** | Cheapest. Heats fast, scorches the wick easily, and the wick's taste comes through. |
The word "ceramic" on a box is not a guarantee of anything by itself — the grade and the porosity vary — but as a category it is the reason most decent cartridges use it.
## Why taste complaints are usually heat complaints

A burnt taste almost always means the element got hot with nothing to heat: the wick was dry, the contents too thick to travel, or the voltage too high for that cartridge. Once the wick has scorched the taste stays, because the damage is to the wick and not to the contents.
Three things avoid it:

- **Let a fresh cartridge stand upright for a few minutes** after fitting, so the wick saturates before power reaches it.
- **Use short draws, spaced out.** Long continuous draws dry the wick faster than it refills.
- **Start at the lowest voltage setting** your battery has and raise it only if it feels weak.
## Why cold makes everything worse

Cold contents are thicker, so they travel to the wick more slowly, so the element is more likely to run dry. A device that has been in a cold car often behaves like a faulty one for its first few draws. Warm it in a pocket first.
The reverse — heat — thins everything, which causes leaks. See [storing a device: heat, light and which way up](/blog/storing-a-device-heat-light-and-which-way-up).
## Resistance, briefly

Cartridges are usually somewhere between 0.8 and 1.8 ohms. Lower resistance draws more current and produces more heat at the same voltage. If a battery offers settings, the practical approach is to start low: too cool tells you nothing is damaged, while too hot has already scorched the wick.

title: What a Blinking Light Usually Means
summary: There is no common standard, but the patterns repeat across manufacturers: three blinks is usually a short or a bad connection, ten or fifteen is usually a flat battery, and a long continuous blink is usually the draw-time cut-off. Rapid blinking while charging means the cell is refusing the charge.
body: Nobody publishes a standard for this and every manufacturer does as it pleases, which is why a blinking light feels like a code you were never given. In practice the patterns are consistent enough to diagnose.
## The common patterns

| Pattern | Usual meaning | What to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 blinks on draw | Short circuit or poor contact | Unscrew the cartridge, wipe both contacts, refit hand tight |
| 10 to 15 blinks | Battery flat | Charge it, if it can be charged |
| One long blink, then off | Draw-time cut-off reached | Shorter draws; this is a safety feature working |
| Rapid blinking on the charger | Cell refusing the charge | Stop charging it and stop using it |
| No light at all | Flat, dead, or no contact | Try another battery or cartridge to isolate it |
## The three-blink case, in order

1. **Unscrew the cartridge and look at the centre pin.** Contents leaked onto the contact is the commonest cause and a cotton bud fixes it.
2. **Refit hand tight.** Over-tightening crushes the pin, which produces exactly the same three blinks permanently.
3. **Try the cartridge on another battery**, and another cartridge on this battery. Whichever combination fails tells you which part is at fault.
## The pattern to take seriously

**Rapid blinking while charging, a hot body, a swollen case, or any smell of burning.** Disconnect it, put it somewhere non-flammable away from anything that can catch, and do not charge it again. A lithium cell that refuses charge is not a fault to work around.
Dispose of it properly rather than in household rubbish. See [disposing of hardware and lithium batteries](/blog/disposing-of-hardware-and-lithium-batteries).
## Where a sealed device leaves you

On a two-part setup these tests take half a minute. On a sealed disposable there is nothing to unscrew and no part to swap, so a blinking light is all the information there is. That is the practical cost of the format. See [disposable or cartridge](/blog/disposable-or-cartridge-what-the-difference-is).
## Before you conclude it is broken

A cold device, a device that has been lying on its side, and a device with a fresh cartridge that has not been left to saturate all behave like faulty ones. Warm it, stand it upright a few minutes, then test again.

title: Charging a Rechargeable Device Safely
summary: Use a low-output USB port rather than a fast phone charger, unplug it when the light says full, and never charge it overnight or on anything soft. These are small lithium cells with minimal protection circuitry, and every serious incident with them involves heat, a fast charger or being left connected.
body: The cell in a small device is nothing like the one in a phone: less capacity, far simpler protection, and no thermal management to speak of. Most of the rules follow from that.
## The short version

- **Use a computer USB port or a low-output wall adapter**, not a fast phone charger. A 5 W output is plenty; a 30 W charger is not a favour.
- **Watch it.** Charge it while you are in the room and awake.
- **Unplug it when the light says full.** These cells sit at full charge without any cut-off you should rely on.
- **Charge it on a hard surface** — a desk or a tile, not a bed, a sofa or a pile of papers.
- **Never overnight.** Every avoidable incident we have read about happened to a device left connected and unattended.
- **Use the right cable.** USB-C to USB-C from a laptop can negotiate a higher voltage than a cheap device expects. A plain USB-A to USB-C cable is the safer choice.
## Temperature

Do not charge a device that is cold from outdoors — let it reach room temperature first, because charging a cold lithium cell damages it. Equally, do not charge one that is already warm. If the body is hot to the touch at any point, disconnect it.

A device that gets hot while charging, swells, or blinks rapidly and refuses to charge should be taken out of use, put somewhere non-flammable, and disposed of properly. See [disposing of hardware and lithium batteries](/blog/disposing-of-hardware-and-lithium-batteries).
## Storage charge

A cell left flat for months may not come back, and one left at full charge for months ages faster. If a device is going in a drawer for a while, leave it around half charged and store it upright somewhere cool. See [storing a device](/blog/storing-a-device-heat-light-and-which-way-up).
## Why a rechargeable disposable exists at all

The battery in a sealed device is sized to the case, not to the contents, so a larger cartridge outlasts its own cell. The USB port exists so the device can finish what it holds rather than die half full. It does not make the cell a good one, and it does not mean the device is designed for long service.
## What not to do

Do not attempt to open a sealed device to reach the cell, do not charge through improvised contacts, and do not carry a loose device in a pocket with keys or coins — a short across the terminals is how these fail dramatically.

title: Storing a Device: Heat, Light and Which Way Up
summary: Upright, mouthpiece up, somewhere cool and dark, around half charged if it is going away for a while. Heat thins the contents and causes leaks, cold thickens them and dries the wick, and a device left on its side floods its own airway.
body: Three variables decide whether a device works properly when you pick it up again: temperature, light and orientation. None of them costs anything to get right.
## Upright, mouthpiece up

A cartridge relies on the wick being fed at a steady rate. Left on its side, contents pool against the airway and the seal; left upside down, they run into the mouthpiece. Both produce the same two complaints — a leak, and a draw that arrives as liquid rather than vapour.
Standing a device upright for a few minutes before use also lets a dry wick reabsorb, which is the fix for the weak first draw people mistake for a fault.
## Temperature

| Condition | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Hot — a car dashboard, a sunny windowsill | Contents thin, seals weep, the cell ages fast |
| Room temperature | Correct |
| Cold — an unheated garage, a winter coat left outside | Contents thicken, the wick struggles, the element scorches |
| Cold then charged immediately | Damages a lithium cell |
A car in summer is the worst place in ordinary life for both the hardware and its contents. A drawer indoors is the best.
## Light

Ultraviolet light degrades most botanical and cannabinoid contents over time, which is why cartridges are often tinted and why a clear one should not live on a windowsill. Dark is not fussiness; it is the difference between a cartridge that tastes the same in three months and one that does not.
## Charge level for storage

For anything going away longer than a couple of weeks, leave a rechargeable cell around half charged. Flat cells sometimes will not revive; full cells age faster. See [charging a rechargeable device safely](/blog/charging-a-rechargeable-device-safely).
## Away from other things

Keep devices out of a pocket or bag with keys and coins, where a short across the terminals is possible, and out of reach of children and animals. Store them separately from anything you would not want to smell of them, because seals weep slowly even when nothing is obviously wrong.
## When a device has been stored badly

Warm it to room temperature, stand it upright for ten minutes, wipe the contacts, then try a short draw. Most devices written off after a cold or hot spell recover with those three steps. A swollen case or a burning smell is different — that one goes for [disposal](/blog/disposing-of-hardware-and-lithium-batteries).

title: Disposing of Hardware and Lithium Batteries
summary: A used device is electronic waste with a lithium cell in it, and it does not belong in household rubbish or a kerbside recycling bin. Take it to a battery collection point, a household hazardous waste site, or a shop that accepts device take-back. Never crush, puncture or bin one.
body: Every sealed device ends its life as a small lithium cell inside a plastic body with residue in it. That combination is the reason bin lorries and recycling facilities catch fire, and the reason this is worth two minutes of attention.
## Why not the bin

A lithium cell that is crushed — which is what happens in a compacting truck or a sorting facility — can go into thermal runaway and ignite. Waste industry fire statistics put battery-caused fires among the leading causes of facility fires, and small sealed devices are disproportionately represented because people bin them without thinking.
Kerbside recycling is not the answer either: those streams are sorted by machinery that does the crushing.
## Where it should go

| Option | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Battery collection bins | Common in supermarkets, hardware and electronics shops |
| Household hazardous waste site | Your council or county site; almost all accept cells |
| Retailer take-back | Some vape and electronics shops accept devices |
| Electronics recycling | Handles the whole device, cell included |
Search for "battery recycling near me" plus your town and you will usually find a collection point within a few miles.
## Before you take it anywhere

- **Do not open it or try to remove the cell.** Puncturing a pouch cell is how people get hurt.
- **Tape over the charging port and any exposed contacts** with a strip of electrical tape, so nothing can short in a bag or a bin.
- **Store it apart from other cells** while it waits — terminal to terminal contact between loose cells is a short.
- **If it is swollen, hot or smells burnt**, keep it away from anything flammable, outside if you can, and take it to a hazardous waste site rather than a shop bin.
## Two-part hardware

A cartridge-and-battery setup produces far less of this. The battery goes on being used across dozens of cartridges, so there is one cell to dispose of instead of dozens. The empty cartridges are mixed plastic and metal — not recyclable in most kerbside streams, but not a fire risk either. See [disposable or cartridge](/blog/disposable-or-cartridge-what-the-difference-is).
## The honest summary

There is no elegant way to dispose of a sealed disposable. The format's convenience is paid for in lithium cells, and the only responsible route is a collection point. If that matters to you, the two-part format is the practical answer rather than a virtuous one.

title: What a Dual Chamber Device Is
summary: Two separate tanks and two heating elements in one body, with a switch that selects which one the battery feeds. It lets one device hold two different contents without mixing them. The trade-off is one cell powering two elements, and twice as many seals that can fail.
body: A dual chamber device is what the name says: two independent tanks in a single body, each with its own element, selected by a switch or a twist of the base.
## What is actually doubled

| Part | Doubled? |
| --- | --- |
| Tank | Yes — two, kept separate |
| Heating element | Yes — one per tank |
| Airway | Usually two, sometimes joined at the mouthpiece |
| Battery | **No** — one cell serves both |
| Charging port | No |

That last pair is the whole trade-off. The cell is the same size as a single-chamber device of similar dimensions, but it has twice as much content to heat, which is why nearly every dual chamber device is rechargeable rather than sealed.
## Why anyone wants one

It solves a specific problem: carrying two different contents without carrying two devices, and switching between them without the first one's taste following the second. Because the tanks never meet, a strong flavour on one side does not carry across.
Some devices allow both chambers at once, blending at the mouthpiece. Whether that is a feature or a muddle depends entirely on what is in them.
## What to check on one

- **Which chamber is selected.** Almost every complaint of "one side does not work" is a switch in the middle position, or a chamber that is simply empty.
- **The selector's feel.** A vague switch that drifts between positions is the commonest mechanical fault in this format.
- **Seals.** Twice the tanks means twice the joints, and a leak from one chamber often contaminates the shared mouthpiece.
- **Charge before judging it.** A single cell running two elements goes flat faster than people expect, and a weak draw on both sides is usually a flat battery. See [charging a rechargeable device safely](/blog/charging-a-rechargeable-device-safely).
## Cleaning the shared parts

If the mouthpiece is shared, it is the one part where the two sides meet. A cotton bud through it between switches keeps each side tasting of itself. Never rinse the body under a tap — there is a cell inside.
## Storage

Upright and cool, like any other device, and more strictly than most: a dual chamber body on its side has two tanks pooling against their seals rather than one. See [storing a device](/blog/storing-a-device-heat-light-and-which-way-up).

title: Why a Cartridge Clogs, and What to Do
summary: A clog is nearly always cold, thick contents blocking a narrow airway, or condensation collecting in the mouthpiece. Warm the cartridge in your hands, stand it upright, clear the mouthpiece with a cotton bud or a paperclip, then take short gentle draws rather than hard ones.
body: A blocked cartridge feels like a broken cartridge and usually is not. The airway in these things is about a millimetre across, and it does not take much to obstruct it.
## The three causes
**Cold, thick contents.** Cold makes everything thicker, and thicker contents move into the airway instead of onto the wick. A device that has been outdoors is the classic case.
**Condensation.** Vapour that cools inside the mouthpiece turns back into liquid and collects there. It builds up with normal use and is the most common cause after cold.

**Hard draws.** Pulling harder floods the airway with more than the element can turn over — which makes the blockage worse, which makes people pull harder still. Short, gentle draws are the whole answer.
## Clearing one, in order

1. **Warm it.** Hold it in a closed hand for two or three minutes, or in a pocket. Never with a hairdryer, a radiator or hot water.
2. **Stand it upright** for a few minutes so the wick reabsorbs and the airway drains back.
3. **Clear the mouthpiece.** A cotton bud for what you can reach; a straightened paperclip, gently, for a deeper plug. Do not ream the element itself.
4. **Take two or three short, gentle draws** with the battery off if the device allows it — the airflow alone shifts most blockages.
5. **Then a short draw with power**, at the lowest voltage setting.
## What makes it worse

| Avoid | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Hard, long draws | Floods the airway and dries the wick at the same time |
| Heating it with a hairdryer or hot water | Damages seals, and a hot cell is a hazard |
| Blowing back into the mouthpiece | Pushes the plug into the element |
| Highest voltage setting | Scorches the wick instead of clearing the airway |
## Avoiding it

Keep the device at room temperature, store it upright, and wipe the mouthpiece with a cotton bud every few days. Short draws spaced out beat long ones. See [storing a device](/blog/storing-a-device-heat-light-and-which-way-up) and [what a coil does](/blog/what-a-coil-does-and-why-material-matters).
## When it is not a clog

No vapour at all plus a blinking light is a power or contact problem, not a blockage — check the contacts and the fit first. See [what a blinking light usually means](/blog/what-a-blinking-light-usually-means). A burnt taste that survives everything above means the wick is scorched, and that does not come back.
